title: WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) categories 1-4 overview
summary: The WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (5th edition, 2015) classify the safety of each contraceptive method for a person with a given characteristic or condition into four categories. Categories 1 and 4 give clear directions; categories 2 and 3 require clinical judgement and access to follow-up.

sections.heading: Categories
items: Category 1: No restriction on use of the method.
Category 2: Advantages generally outweigh risks; the method can generally be used, with some additional follow-up.

Category 3: Risks usually outweigh advantages; method usually not recommended unless other methods are unavailable or unacceptable, and requires careful clinical judgement and access to clinical services.
Category 4: Unacceptable health risk; the method should NOT be used.

sections.heading: How to apply
items: Where resources for clinical judgement are limited, simplify to 2 categories: category 1-2 = use the method; category 3-4 = do not use the method.
Categories apply separately to starting (initiation) and to continuing a method in someone who develops a condition.
Always combine MEC with counselling on effectiveness, side effects and STI protection.

redFlags: Never start or continue a category 4 method (e.g. combined hormonal contraception in migraine with aura).

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 5th ed (2015)

title: Combined oral contraceptive (COC) pill
summary: Combined oral contraceptives contain an oestrogen and a progestogen, taken daily to suppress ovulation. Typical-use failure is about 7-9 per 100 women per year; perfect use is far lower. Suitable for many people but contraindicated where oestrogen risk is unacceptable.

sections.heading: Eligibility (selected WHO MEC)
items: Category 1-2 for most healthy non-smoking women under 35.
Category 4 (do not use): migraine with aura at any age; current breast cancer; <6 weeks postpartum and breastfeeding; known thrombogenic mutations; current/history of VTE or arterial disease.
Category 3-4 with smoking >=15 cigarettes/day at age >=35, and with uncontrolled hypertension.

steps.detail: Ideally on day 1 of the menstrual cycle for immediate cover; if started after day 5, use a backup method (e.g. condoms) for 7 days.
One pill at the same time each day. With 21-day packs take for 21 days then a 7-day break; with 28-day packs take continuously.
If one pill is >24h late, take it as soon as remembered and continue; if 2 or more missed, use backup for 7 days and consider emergency contraception per pack/FSRH advice.

redFlags: New severe headache, focal neurological symptoms, unilateral leg swelling/pain, chest pain or breathlessness - stop and assess for VTE/arterial event.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 5th ed (2015)
FSRH Combined Hormonal Contraception guideline

title: Progestogen-only pill (POP)
summary: The progestogen-only pill contains only a progestogen and avoids oestrogen-related risks, making it a useful option in breastfeeding, migraine with aura, VTE history and smokers over 35. Desogestrel POPs inhibit ovulation; traditional POPs act mainly on cervical mucus.

sections.heading: Eligibility
items: WHO MEC category 1-2 for the great majority of women, including those with migraine with aura, controlled hypertension, VTE history and breastfeeding from birth.
Useful where oestrogen is contraindicated.
Few absolute contraindications (e.g. current breast cancer = category 4).

steps.detail: One pill every day with no pill-free break.
Traditional POPs must be taken within 3 hours of the usual time; desogestrel POPs allow a 12-hour window.
If taken outside the window, take it at once, continue, and use a backup method for 48 hours; consider emergency contraception if intercourse occurred.

redFlags: New breast lump or unexplained vaginal bleeding warrants assessment.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 5th ed (2015)
FSRH Progestogen-only Pills guideline

title: DMPA injectable (depot medroxyprogesterone acetate)
summary: DMPA is a long-acting progestogen-only injectable. The intramuscular formulation is 150 mg given every 12-13 weeks (a subcutaneous 104 mg formulation also exists). It is highly effective, with perfect-use failure under 1 per 100 women per year.

sections.heading: Eligibility
items: WHO MEC category 1-2 for most women; useful where oestrogen is contraindicated.
Category 3 in some settings: unexplained vaginal bleeding before evaluation; multiple cardiovascular risk factors; severe hypertension.
Associated with reversible loss of bone mineral density that largely recovers after stopping.

steps.detail: Give within the first 7 days of the cycle for immediate cover; otherwise use backup for 7 days.
Re-inject every 12-13 weeks (IM DMPA 150 mg).
If more than 2 weeks late, exclude pregnancy and advise backup contraception for 7 days after the injection.

redFlags: Counsel on delayed return of fertility (may take several months to over a year after stopping).

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 5th ed (2015)
FSRH Progestogen-only Injectable guideline

title: Etonogestrel subdermal implant
summary: The single-rod etonogestrel implant is a long-acting reversible contraceptive (LARC) inserted subdermally in the upper arm, licensed for 3 years. It is among the most effective methods, with failure well under 1 per 100 women per year, and is rapidly reversible.

sections.heading: Eligibility
items: WHO MEC category 1-2 for the vast majority of women, including most with cardiovascular risk and migraine with aura.
Progestogen-only, so suitable when oestrogen is contraindicated.
Current breast cancer is category 4.

steps.detail: Insert subdermally in the non-dominant upper arm during days 1-5 of the cycle for immediate cover; otherwise use backup for 7 days.
Effective for 3 years (licensed duration); remove and replace at or before 3 years.
Palpate before removal; refer if non-palpable. Fertility returns rapidly after removal.

redFlags: Non-palpable implant requires imaging/specialist removal - do not attempt blind removal.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 5th ed (2015)
FSRH Progestogen-only Implant guideline

title: Copper intrauterine device (Cu-IUD)
summary: The copper IUD is a long-acting, hormone-free, reversible contraceptive licensed for up to 10 years (depending on device). It is highly effective (failure under 1 per 100 women per year) and is also the most effective method of emergency contraception.

sections.heading: Eligibility
items: WHO MEC category 1-2 for most women, including those who cannot use hormones.
Category 4 (do not insert): pregnancy; current pelvic infection / purulent cervicitis; unexplained vaginal bleeding before evaluation; gestational trophoblastic disease with high hCG.
May increase menstrual bleeding and cramping.

steps.detail: Insert any time pregnancy can be reasonably excluded; effective immediately.
Leave in place for the licensed duration (up to 10 years for many copper devices).
Teach the woman to feel for threads; review if threads not felt, abnormal pain or abnormal bleeding.

redFlags: Pelvic pain, fever and discharge after insertion suggest pelvic infection. Missing threads with possible pregnancy require urgent review (ectopic risk).

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 5th ed (2015)
FSRH Intrauterine Contraception guideline

title: Levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS)
summary: The levonorgestrel intrauterine system releases progestogen locally, providing highly effective long-acting reversible contraception and reducing menstrual blood loss. Licensed duration depends on device and indication (commonly 5-8 years for contraception with the 52 mg system).

sections.heading: Eligibility
items: WHO MEC category 1-2 for most women.
Useful for heavy menstrual bleeding and as the progestogen component of HRT (52 mg system).
Category 4: pregnancy, current pelvic infection, current breast cancer, unexplained vaginal bleeding before evaluation.

steps.detail: Insert when pregnancy can be excluded; if inserted after day 7 of the cycle, use backup for 7 days.
Use for the licensed duration of the specific device for contraception.
Counsel that irregular bleeding/spotting is common early and that periods usually become lighter or stop.

redFlags: Pelvic infection signs after insertion or missing threads with possible pregnancy require urgent review.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 5th ed (2015)
FSRH Intrauterine Contraception guideline

title: Male and female (external/internal) condoms
summary: Condoms are barrier methods that prevent pregnancy and reduce transmission of HIV and other sexually transmitted infections. Typical-use pregnancy rates are about 13-21 per 100 women per year, so they are most reliable when used correctly with every act and may be combined with another method.

sections.heading: Key points
items: Only method that also reduces STI/HIV transmission - recommend dual protection alongside hormonal/LARC methods.
Use a new condom for every act of intercourse.
Avoid oil-based lubricants with latex condoms; use water- or silicone-based lubricant.

steps.detail: Check expiry date and that packaging is intact; open carefully without teeth or nails.
External condom: place on erect penis before any genital contact, pinching the tip to expel air. Internal condom: insert into vagina before intercourse per instructions.
Withdraw while still erect holding the base; remove, knot and dispose. If it breaks or slips, consider emergency contraception and STI risk.

redFlags: Condom breakage/slippage with pregnancy or HIV risk - offer emergency contraception and HIV post-exposure prophylaxis assessment promptly.

references.label: WHO/UNFPA male latex condom specification and guidance

title: Emergency contraception: levonorgestrel 1.5 mg
summary: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg orally as a single dose is an oral emergency contraceptive used after unprotected or inadequately protected intercourse. It works mainly by delaying ovulation and is more effective the sooner it is taken.

sections.heading: Use
items: Single dose of levonorgestrel 1.5 mg taken as soon as possible.
WHO states it can be used up to 120 hours after intercourse, but effectiveness declines with time and it is best within 72 hours.
A copper IUD is more effective and should be offered where appropriate; ulipristal acetate is an alternative oral option.

steps.detail: It is not 100% effective and is less effective than a copper IUD; take as early as possible.
If vomiting occurs within 2-3 hours, repeat the dose.
Start or continue ongoing contraception; do a pregnancy test if the next period is more than 7 days late.

redFlags: Does not protect against pregnancy from later intercourse in the same cycle; offer ongoing contraception.

references.label: WHO Emergency contraception fact sheet
FSRH Emergency Contraception guideline

title: Emergency contraception: ulipristal acetate 30 mg
summary: Ulipristal acetate 30 mg orally as a single dose is a selective progesterone receptor modulator for emergency contraception, effective up to 120 hours after unprotected intercourse. It is generally more effective than levonorgestrel, particularly nearer ovulation.

sections.heading: Use
items: Single 30 mg dose taken as soon as possible, up to 120 hours (5 days) after intercourse.
Preferred oral option when more than 72 hours have elapsed or near the time of ovulation.
A copper IUD remains the most effective emergency method.

steps.detail: Avoid starting/continuing hormonal contraception for 5 days after ulipristal, as progestogens may reduce its effectiveness; use condoms until restarting.
Repeat the dose if vomiting occurs within 3 hours.
Advise expressing and discarding breast milk for 1 week after ulipristal.

redFlags: Do pregnancy test if period is more than 7 days late; ulipristal is not recommended in severe hepatic impairment or with repeated use in the same cycle without advice.

references.label: WHO Emergency contraception fact sheet
FSRH Emergency Contraception guideline

title: Emergency contraception: copper IUD
summary: Insertion of a copper IUD is the most effective method of emergency contraception, with a failure rate around 0.1%, and provides ongoing contraception. It can be inserted within 5 days of unprotected intercourse or within 5 days of the earliest estimated ovulation.

sections.heading: Use
items: Most effective emergency method - offer to all women requesting emergency contraception where appropriate.
Insert within 120 hours of the first unprotected intercourse, or up to 5 days after the earliest likely ovulation.
Provides ongoing long-acting contraception once in place.

steps.detail: Screen for STI risk; provide treatment/prophylaxis as indicated but do not delay insertion unnecessarily.
Insert the copper device using standard aseptic technique.
Explain it can stay as ongoing contraception or be removed after the next period if not wanted long term.

redFlags: Current pelvic infection or confirmed existing pregnancy are contraindications to insertion.

references.label: WHO Emergency contraception fact sheet
FSRH Emergency Contraception guideline

title: Lactational amenorrhoea method (LAM)
summary: LAM is a temporary, natural method that uses breastfeeding-induced suppression of ovulation. When all three criteria are met it is about 98% effective up to 6 months postpartum.

sections.heading: Three criteria (ALL must be met)
items: The mother is fully or nearly fully (exclusively) breastfeeding, day and night.
Menstruation has not returned (amenorrhoea).
The infant is less than 6 months old.

steps.detail: Advise starting another contraceptive method before any criterion is no longer met.
If menses return, breastfeeding reduces, or the baby reaches 6 months, LAM is no longer reliable.
LAM does not protect against STIs; advise condoms if at risk.

redFlags: Effectiveness falls sharply once any of the three criteria is lost - transition promptly to another method.

references.label: WHO Postpartum Family Planning: Lactational Amenorrhea Method

title: Fertility awareness-based methods (FABM)
summary: Fertility awareness methods identify the fertile window using indicators such as calendar/standard days, cervical mucus and basal body temperature, so the couple avoids unprotected intercourse during fertile days. Typical-use failure is relatively high (often quoted around 15-25 per 100 women per year) and depends heavily on correct, consistent use.

sections.heading: Method types
items: Calendar/standard days method (e.g. avoid intercourse on cycle days 8-19 for regular 26-32 day cycles).
Cervical mucus (Billings/two-day) method tracking secretions.
Symptothermal method combining temperature and mucus signs.

steps.detail: Requires instruction and accurate daily recording to identify the fertile window.
Abstain or use a barrier method during identified fertile days.
Less reliable with irregular cycles, illness, breastfeeding or shift work; offer more effective methods if pregnancy must be avoided.

redFlags: Not suitable as sole method when avoiding pregnancy is critical; provides no STI protection.

references.label: WHO Family planning/contraception methods

title: Female sterilisation (tubal ligation/occlusion)
summary: Tubal ligation or occlusion is a permanent surgical method that interrupts the fallopian tubes. It is highly effective (failure under 1 per 100 women) but should be considered irreversible, so counselling on permanence is essential.

sections.heading: Counselling
items: Intended as a permanent method - ensure the decision is informed and free of coercion.
Discuss highly effective reversible LARC alternatives (implant, IUD/IUS) which match or exceed effectiveness.
Provides no STI protection.

steps.detail: Obtain informed consent with clear understanding of permanence and small failure/ectopic risk.
Performed surgically (e.g. laparoscopic or postpartum mini-laparotomy).
Use effective contraception until the procedure is confirmed; counsel that any pregnancy after failure carries increased ectopic risk.

redFlags: Any pregnancy after tubal sterilisation - assess urgently for ectopic pregnancy.

references.label: WHO Family planning/contraception methods

title: Vasectomy (male sterilisation)
summary: Vasectomy is a permanent, highly effective method in which the vas deferens is occluded. It is simpler, safer and cheaper than female sterilisation, but is not immediately effective and should be considered irreversible.

sections.heading: Counselling
items: Permanent method - confirm completed family/informed choice.
Not effective immediately: residual sperm persist for weeks.
Provides no STI protection.

steps.detail: Minor procedure (often no-scalpel technique) under local anaesthetic.
Use another contraceptive method until clearance, typically until a post-procedure semen analysis confirms azoospermia (around 12 weeks).
Do not rely on vasectomy until the confirmatory semen test shows no motile sperm.

redFlags: Do not stop other contraception until confirmatory semen analysis shows clearance.

references.label: WHO Family planning/contraception methods

title: Contraception in specific conditions (HTN, migraine, VTE, breastfeeding, HIV)
summary: Method choice should be guided by the WHO MEC for the individual's conditions. Progestogen-only methods and non-hormonal options are generally safe where oestrogen is contraindicated.

sections.heading: Condition-specific guidance (WHO MEC)
items: Migraine with aura: combined hormonal contraception is category 4 (do not use); progestogen-only methods and copper IUD are appropriate.
Hypertension: uncontrolled/severe hypertension is category 3-4 for combined methods; progestogen-only and copper IUD are generally suitable.
Personal history of VTE / thrombophilia: combined hormonal contraception category 4; offer progestogen-only or copper IUD.
Breastfeeding: combined methods restricted in early postpartum (category 3-4 in first 6 weeks); progestogen-only methods can be started from birth.

HIV: most methods are category 1-2; check drug interactions with enzyme-inducing antiretrovirals (e.g. efavirenz) which may reduce efficacy of some hormonal methods - condoms still essential for transmission prevention.

redFlags: Combined hormonal contraception is unacceptable (category 4) in migraine with aura, VTE history/thrombophilia and severe/uncontrolled hypertension.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 5th ed (2015)

title: WHO AWaRe antibiotic classification in stewardship
summary: The WHO AWaRe classification groups antibiotics into Access, Watch and Reserve to guide appropriate use and monitor stewardship. WHO recommends at least 60% of total antibiotic use be from the Access group.

sections.heading: Groups
items: Access: first/second-choice antibiotics for common infections with narrower spectrum and lower resistance potential (e.g. amoxicillin); should make up most of use.
Watch: broader-spectrum agents with higher resistance potential (e.g. ciprofloxacin, ceftriaxone); key targets for stewardship and monitoring.
Reserve: last-resort agents (e.g. colistin, linezolid for resistant Gram-positives) for confirmed/suspected multidrug-resistant infections.

sections.heading: Practice
items: Prefer Access-group agents whenever clinically appropriate.
Restrict and review Watch/Reserve agents; require senior/specialist sign-off for Reserve.
Use AWaRe metrics to monitor and set targets (WHO national target: >=60% Access).

references.label: WHO AWaRe (Access, Watch, Reserve) classification of antibiotics 2023/2025

title: Start Smart Then Focus antimicrobial prescribing
summary: Start Smart Then Focus is the UK antimicrobial stewardship framework: start antibiotics appropriately when indicated, then review at 48-72 hours and decide a clear outcome. It underpins NICE NG15 systems for effective antimicrobial use.

sections.heading: Start Smart
items: Do not start antibiotics without clinical evidence of bacterial infection.
Take cultures before starting where possible.
Document indication, drug, dose, route and planned duration/review date; follow local guidelines and obtain senior advice for broad-spectrum agents.

sections.heading: Then Focus (48-72h review)
items: Review clinical diagnosis and continuing need, using microbiology results.
Choose one documented outcome: Stop; Switch IV to oral; Change (e.g. de-escalate); Continue (with review date); or refer to OPAT.
Always document the review decision.

references.label: UKHSA Start Smart Then Focus antimicrobial stewardship toolkit
NICE NG15 Antimicrobial stewardship: systems and processes

title: IV-to-oral antibiotic switch criteria
summary: Switching from intravenous to oral antibiotics when criteria are met reduces line complications, length of stay and cost without compromising outcomes. Review IV therapy daily.

sections.heading: Criteria for switch
items: Clinically improving and haemodynamically stable.
Afebrile (commonly for >24 hours) with improving inflammatory markers.
Able to tolerate and absorb oral medication (functioning GI tract, no malabsorption/vomiting).
A suitable oral agent with adequate bioavailability is available and there is no deep-seated infection mandating IV (e.g. endocarditis, CNS infection, undrained collection).

redFlags: Do not switch in infections requiring sustained high tissue levels (e.g. endocarditis, meningitis, Staph aureus bacteraemia) without specialist advice.

references.label: UKHSA Start Smart Then Focus / IV to oral switch (IVOS) criteria

title: Antibiotic review at 48-72 hours and duration
summary: All antibiotic courses should have a documented review at 48-72 hours and the shortest effective duration. Avoid reflexively continuing antibiotics; longer courses increase resistance and C. difficile risk.

sections.heading: Review actions
items: Reassess at 48-72 hours when most cultures and clinical trajectory are clearer.
Stop if infection is unlikely; de-escalate to narrowest effective agent; switch IV to oral if appropriate.
Set and document a stop/review date; use the shortest evidence-based course.

sections.heading: Duration principles
items: Many common infections need only short courses; follow local/NICE guideline durations.
Longer is not safer - prolonged courses drive resistance and C. difficile.
Reassess at the planned review date rather than automatically completing arbitrary long courses.

references.label: NICE NG15 Antimicrobial stewardship

title: Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis timing and duration
summary: Surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis reduces surgical site infection when the right agent is given at the right time. WHO recommends administration within 120 minutes before incision, accounting for the antibiotic half-life, and against prolonging prophylaxis after surgery.

sections.heading: Timing and dosing
items: Administer within 120 minutes before skin incision; for short half-life agents (cephalosporins, penicillins) give closer to incision (within 60 minutes).
Redose intra-operatively for long procedures or major blood loss per agent half-life.
Use weight-adjusted dosing where indicated.

sections.heading: Duration
items: A single dose is sufficient for most procedures.
WHO recommends against continuing prophylaxis after wound closure to prevent SSI.
Prolonged post-operative prophylaxis does not reduce SSI and increases resistance and C. difficile risk.

redFlags: Avoid prophylaxis given too early (>120 min before incision) or continued unnecessarily after surgery.

references.label: WHO Global guidelines for the prevention of surgical site infection

title: Antibiotic de-escalation
summary: De-escalation means narrowing empirical broad-spectrum therapy to the narrowest effective agent once culture and sensitivity results are available, or stopping if infection is excluded. It is a core component of the 48-72 hour review.

steps.detail: At 48-72 hours review culture, sensitivity and clinical response.
Switch from broad-spectrum empirical therapy to a targeted narrow-spectrum agent guided by susceptibility.
Stop antibiotics if infection is unlikely and limit total duration to the shortest effective course.

references.label: NICE NG15 Antimicrobial stewardship

title: Penicillin allergy de-labelling
summary: Most patients labelled penicillin-allergic are not truly allergic, and the label drives use of broader, less effective, costlier antibiotics with worse outcomes. Structured allergy history and de-labelling improve prescribing.

sections.heading: Assessment
items: Take a detailed history: nature, timing and severity of the reaction and how long ago it occurred.
Low-risk features (isolated non-specific rash, GI upset, remote vague history, family-only history) may allow de-labelling or referral for testing.
High-risk features (anaphylaxis, severe cutaneous adverse reactions such as SJS/TEN/DRESS) require specialist allergy assessment - do not re-challenge.

sections.heading: Action
items: Refer appropriate patients for allergy assessment / oral challenge per local pathways.
Document outcome clearly and update the allergy record.
Correct de-labelling restores access to first-line narrow-spectrum agents.

redFlags: Never re-challenge a patient with a history of anaphylaxis or severe cutaneous adverse reaction without specialist allergy input.

references.label: NICE Drug allergy: diagnosis and management (CG183)

title: C. difficile-sparing antibiotic prescribing
summary: Several antibiotic classes carry a high risk of precipitating Clostridioides difficile infection. Minimising their use, especially in elderly and hospitalised patients, reduces C. difficile incidence.

sections.heading: Higher-risk antibiotics (the '4 Cs')
items: Clindamycin.
Cephalosporins (especially broad-spectrum).
Co-amoxiclav.
Ciprofloxacin and other fluoroquinolones.

sections.heading: Stewardship actions
items: Prefer narrow-spectrum alternatives where clinically appropriate.
Avoid unnecessarily long courses and broad-spectrum use, particularly in older adults.
Review and de-escalate at 48-72 hours.

redFlags: New diarrhoea on or after antibiotics - consider C. difficile, send stool, review antibiotics and isolate per local policy.

references.label: NICE Clostridioides difficile infection: antimicrobial prescribing (NG199)

title: Take cultures before antibiotics
summary: Obtaining appropriate microbiological samples before the first antibiotic dose improves diagnosis, enables targeted therapy and supports de-escalation, without unduly delaying treatment in sepsis.

sections.heading: Principles
items: Send relevant cultures (e.g. blood cultures, urine, sputum, wound swabs) before starting antibiotics where feasible.
In sepsis, take blood cultures but do NOT delay antibiotics beyond recommended timeframes (give within 1 hour for high-risk sepsis).
Results guide later de-escalation to a narrow-spectrum agent.

redFlags: In sepsis/septic shock, do not let culture-taking delay timely empirical antibiotics.

references.label: NICE NG15 Antimicrobial stewardship

title: Biomarker (procalcitonin)-guided antibiotic stopping
summary: Procalcitonin (PCT)-guided protocols can safely reduce antibiotic duration in selected patients (e.g. lower respiratory tract infection, critically ill adults with sepsis) when combined with clinical judgement, without increasing mortality.

sections.heading: Use
items: Used as an adjunct to, not a replacement for, clinical assessment.
Falling PCT (commonly a large reduction from peak, or a low absolute level) supports stopping antibiotics in stable, improving patients.
Demonstrated to shorten antibiotic courses and reduce C. difficile/resistant organism events in sepsis trials.

redFlags: Do not continue antibiotics solely because of a raised biomarker, nor stop in clinically deteriorating patients regardless of PCT.

references.label: NICE DG18 Procalcitonin testing for diagnosing and monitoring sepsis

title: Narrow-spectrum antibiotic preference
summary: Choosing the narrowest effective antibiotic that covers the likely or proven pathogen reduces collateral damage to the microbiome, resistance selection and C. difficile risk.

sections.heading: Principles
items: Match empirical choice to the most likely pathogens and local resistance patterns.
Reserve broad-spectrum agents for severe/undifferentiated sepsis or known resistant organisms.
Once cultures are available, de-escalate to the narrowest effective agent.

references.label: WHO AWaRe classification of antibiotics

title: Outpatient parenteral antimicrobial therapy (OPAT) basics
summary: OPAT delivers IV antimicrobials outside hospital for selected stable patients needing prolonged parenteral therapy, reducing admissions while maintaining safety through structured selection and monitoring.

sections.heading: Patient selection
items: Clinically stable patient with an infection requiring IV therapy who does not need other inpatient care.
Safe home/social environment and reliable vascular access.
Agreed monitoring plan (clinical review and bloods) and clear escalation pathway.

sections.heading: Governance
items: Specialist infection input to confirm diagnosis, agent and duration.
Regular review for efficacy, toxicity and line complications.
Defined criteria for IV-to-oral switch and stopping.

redFlags: Fever, line-site infection or clinical deterioration on OPAT requires prompt clinical review/readmission.

references.label: BSAC/BIA Good practice recommendations for OPAT in adults

title: WHO analgesic ladder for pain relief
summary: The WHO analgesic ladder provides a stepwise approach to pain, escalating from non-opioids to weak then strong opioids according to severity, with adjuvants at any step. Analgesics should be given by mouth, by the clock and by the ladder.

sections.heading: Steps
items: Step 1 (mild pain): non-opioid (paracetamol and/or NSAID) +/- adjuvant.
Step 2 (mild-moderate pain): weak opioid (e.g. codeine, tramadol) + non-opioid +/- adjuvant.
Step 3 (moderate-severe pain): strong opioid (e.g. morphine) + non-opioid +/- adjuvant.

sections.heading: Principles
items: By mouth: use the oral route where possible.
By the clock: give regularly at fixed intervals, not only as required.
By the ladder: step up if pain persists; add adjuvants (e.g. for neuropathic or bone pain) at any step.
Tailor to the individual and review regularly.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the pharmacological and radiotherapeutic management of cancer pain

title: Strong opioid initiation and titration
summary: Oral morphine is first-line for moderate-to-severe pain in palliative care. Start low, provide regular plus as-needed (rescue) doses, and titrate to effect while pre-empting side effects.

steps.detail: Use oral morphine first-line (immediate- and/or sustained-release) in patients without renal failure.
A typical opioid-naive starting schedule is around 20-30 mg oral morphine per 24 hours (e.g. 10-15 mg sustained-release twice daily), with immediate-release morphine for rescue doses.
Prescribe a regular laxative and antiemetic cover, and counsel on drowsiness.
Review pain and rescue-dose use frequently (e.g. daily).
Increase the regular dose based on total opioid used (regular plus rescue) over 24 hours, typically in increments of around 30-50%.
Seek specialist palliative care advice if pain is uncontrolled or dose escalation is rapid.

redFlags: Reduced respiratory rate, pinpoint pupils and increasing drowsiness suggest opioid toxicity - hold opioid and consider naloxone if severe.

references.label: NICE CG140 Palliative care for adults: strong opioids for pain relief

title: Breakthrough pain (rescue) dosing
summary: Breakthrough pain is a transient flare on a background of controlled pain. It is treated with an immediate-release rescue dose proportionate to the regular opioid dose.

sections.heading: Rescue dosing
items: Use an immediate-release opioid (e.g. oral morphine) for breakthrough pain.
A common rescue dose is about one-tenth to one-sixth of the total regular 24-hour opioid dose.
Repeat as needed and review the regular dose if rescue doses are frequently required.

sections.heading: Review
items: Count rescue doses used in 24 hours to inform regular dose titration.
Frequent breakthrough dosing usually means the background dose needs increasing.
Match rescue dose to the regular opioid (recalculate after any background dose change).

references.label: NICE CG140 Palliative care for adults: strong opioids for pain relief

title: Opioid conversion principles
summary: Switching opioids or routes requires using approximate equianalgesic ratios, then reducing the calculated dose to account for incomplete cross-tolerance, and titrating to response. Errors in conversion can cause fatal overdose.

sections.heading: Principles
items: Calculate the total 24-hour dose of the current opioid, then convert using an equianalgesic table or local guideline.
Reduce the calculated equivalent dose (commonly by 25-50%) for incomplete cross-tolerance when switching opioid, then titrate to effect.
Oral-to-subcutaneous morphine is approximately a 2:1 ratio (halve the oral dose for the SC dose).
Always provide an appropriate rescue dose with any new regimen.

redFlags: Conversion errors can be fatal - double-check calculations, use trusted tables, and seek specialist advice for high doses, methadone or fentanyl patches.

references.label: NICE CG140 Palliative care for adults: strong opioids for pain relief

title: Neuropathic pain in palliative care
summary: Neuropathic pain (burning, shooting, with abnormal sensation) often responds poorly to opioids alone and is treated with adjuvant analgesics alongside the analgesic ladder.

sections.heading: Management
items: First-line adjuvants: a tricyclic antidepressant (e.g. amitriptyline), or an anticonvulsant such as gabapentin or pregabalin, or duloxetine.
Titrate adjuvants gradually to balance efficacy and side effects.
Continue background analgesia per the WHO ladder; opioids may still help partially.

sections.heading: Escalation
items: Combine agents from different classes if a single agent is insufficient.
Consider specialist palliative or pain team referral for refractory pain (e.g. ketamine, nerve blocks).
Treat reversible causes (e.g. nerve compression with corticosteroids/radiotherapy where appropriate).

references.label: NICE Neuropathic pain in adults: pharmacological management (CG173)

title: Nausea and vomiting in palliative care
summary: Nausea and vomiting are common and distressing. Management is guided by the likely underlying cause and mechanism, choosing an antiemetic acting at the relevant receptors.

sections.heading: Cause-directed choice
items: Chemical/metabolic (e.g. opioids, hypercalcaemia, uraemia): haloperidol or levomepromazine.
Gastric stasis/functional bowel: a prokinetic such as metoclopramide (avoid in complete bowel obstruction).
Raised intracranial pressure: dexamethasone +/- cyclizine.
Vestibular/motion-related: cyclizine.

sections.heading: Principles
items: Identify and treat reversible causes (e.g. constipation, hypercalcaemia, drugs).
Give antiemetics regularly, not just as needed; use the parenteral/subcutaneous route if vomiting prevents oral intake.
Review and consider broad-spectrum antiemetics (e.g. levomepromazine) if first choice fails.

references.label: WHO palliative care

title: Opioid-induced constipation
summary: Constipation is an almost universal opioid side effect and, unlike many effects, does not develop tolerance. Laxatives should be co-prescribed with regular opioids and titrated to effect.

sections.heading: Management
items: Co-prescribe a regular laxative when starting strong opioids.
Typically use a stimulant laxative (e.g. senna) +/- a softener/osmotic agent; titrate to a comfortable bowel pattern.
Encourage hydration and mobility where feasible; review diet.

sections.heading: If refractory
items: Reassess for impaction or bowel obstruction.
Consider a peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonist (e.g. methylnaltrexone) for opioid-induced constipation resistant to standard laxatives.
Seek specialist advice if no response.

redFlags: Distinguish constipation from bowel obstruction (colicky pain, vomiting, no flatus) before giving stimulant laxatives.

references.label: WHO palliative care

title: Breathlessness (dyspnoea) management in palliative care
summary: Breathlessness is a common, frightening symptom near end of life. Management combines treating reversible causes, non-pharmacological measures and low-dose opioids, with benzodiazepines for associated anxiety.

sections.heading: Non-pharmacological
items: Use a handheld fan or cool air directed at the face.
Position upright, pace activities, and use breathing/relaxation techniques.
Reassure and address anxiety; involve carers.

sections.heading: Pharmacological
items: Low-dose oral or subcutaneous opioid (e.g. morphine) reduces the sensation of breathlessness.
Add a benzodiazepine (e.g. lorazepam) for anxiety-related breathlessness.
Oxygen helps mainly if the patient is hypoxic - it is not routinely beneficial in non-hypoxic breathlessness.

redFlags: Treat reversible causes (e.g. pleural effusion, infection, pulmonary embolism, heart failure) where appropriate to goals of care.

references.label: WHO palliative care

title: Terminal respiratory secretions ('death rattle')
summary: Noisy upper-airway secretions are common in the last days/hours of life as the patient becomes too weak to clear them. They are usually more distressing to relatives than to the patient.

sections.heading: Management
items: Reposition the patient (e.g. on the side) to aid drainage.
Provide reassurance and explanation to family that the patient is usually not distressed.
Consider an antimuscarinic (e.g. hyoscine hydrobromide/butylbromide or glycopyrronium) to reduce new secretions.
Review/stop if secretions persist and remain distressing after about 12 hours, monitoring for delirium, agitation or excess sedation.

redFlags: Monitor for antimuscarinic side effects (delirium, agitation, urinary retention, excessive sedation).

references.label: NICE NG31 Care of dying adults in the last days of life

title: Terminal agitation and delirium
summary: Agitation and delirium are common at the end of life. Management starts by seeking reversible causes, then uses non-drug measures and, if needed, pharmacological sedation.

sections.heading: Assess and treat causes
items: Look for reversible causes: pain, urinary retention, constipation, infection, hypoxia, drug toxicity (including opioid neurotoxicity).

sections.heading: Management
items: Provide calm environment, orientation, presence of family and reassurance.
If pharmacological treatment is needed, an antipsychotic such as haloperidol or levomepromazine is commonly used for delirium/agitation.
A benzodiazepine (e.g. midazolam) may be added for severe agitation or where sedation is the goal.
Seek specialist palliative care advice for refractory symptoms.

redFlags: Sudden severe agitation may indicate a reversible cause (e.g. retention, pain, opioid toxicity) - assess before escalating sedation.

references.label: NICE NG31 Care of dying adults in the last days of life

title: Anticipatory ('just in case') prescribing
summary: Anticipatory prescribing makes medicines available in advance so symptoms in the last days of life can be treated promptly without delay. It is individualised, with documented indications and doses.

sections.heading: Typical symptom cover
items: Pain: a strong opioid (e.g. morphine) subcutaneously as required.
Breathlessness: opioid +/- benzodiazepine.
Nausea/vomiting: an antiemetic (e.g. haloperidol, levomepromazine, cyclizine).
Agitation/anxiety: a benzodiazepine (e.g. midazolam).
Respiratory secretions: an antimuscarinic (e.g. hyoscine, glycopyrronium).

sections.heading: Principles
items: Individualise to the person's likely symptoms and renal/hepatic function.
Specify clear indications, doses, route (often subcutaneous) and maximum frequency.
Ensure access to administration and review effectiveness regularly.

references.label: NICE NG31 Care of dying adults in the last days of life

title: Continuous subcutaneous infusion (syringe driver) basics
summary: A syringe driver delivers a continuous subcutaneous infusion of medicines over 24 hours when the oral route is unreliable (e.g. vomiting, dysphagia, reduced consciousness in last days of life). It maintains steady symptom control.

sections.heading: Indications
items: Persistent nausea/vomiting, dysphagia or inability to swallow.
Reduced consciousness or the last days of life when oral medicines are not feasible.
Need for steady drug levels for symptom control.

sections.heading: Practice
items: Convert oral doses to the subcutaneous equivalent (e.g. oral-to-SC morphine approximately 2:1).
Provide as-needed (breakthrough) subcutaneous doses in addition to the infusion.
Check drug compatibility before combining medicines, monitor the site for inflammation, and review the regimen regularly.

redFlags: Check compatibility of combined drugs; inspect the infusion site for redness/swelling and replace if reaction occurs.

references.label: NICE NG31 Care of dying adults in the last days of life

title: Mouth care in palliative and end-of-life care
summary: Good mouth care relieves dryness and discomfort and prevents complications, and is especially important as oral intake declines near the end of life. Hydration needs are assessed and supported as part of comfort care.

sections.heading: Care measures
items: Keep the mouth clean and moist with regular oral care and sips/sponges of water as tolerated.
Apply lip balm to prevent cracking; offer ice chips or saliva substitutes for dry mouth.
Treat oral candidiasis (e.g. with an antifungal) and other reversible causes of mouth pain.
Involve and teach family carers to provide gentle mouth care.

references.label: NICE NG31 Care of dying adults in the last days of life

title: Care in the last days of life
summary: Care of dying adults in the last days of life focuses on recognising dying, communicating with the patient and family, individualised symptom control, hydration review and shared decision-making.

sections.heading: Key elements
items: Recognise when a person may be entering the last days of life and review regularly.
Communicate sensitively and honestly with the dying person (if able) and those important to them.
Provide individualised symptom control and anticipatory medicines.
Assess hydration needs and support assisted hydration where appropriate to comfort and wishes.
Review and stop non-essential medicines/interventions; document an individual care plan.

redFlags: Avoid both under-treatment of distressing symptoms and inappropriate burdensome interventions; reassess if the person stabilises or improves.

references.label: NICE NG31 Care of dying adults in the last days of life

title: Advance care planning
summary: Advance care planning is a voluntary process of discussing and recording a person's values, goals and preferences for future care, used if they later lose capacity. It supports care aligned with the person's wishes.

sections.heading: Components
items: Explore the person's understanding, values, goals and fears about future care.
Discuss preferences for treatment, place of care/death and resuscitation.
Identify a substitute decision-maker / lasting power of attorney where applicable.
Document and share decisions (e.g. advance statements, advance decisions to refuse treatment) with the care team.

sections.heading: Principles
items: Voluntary, patient-centred and revisited as the situation changes.
Conducted with capacity assessment and good communication.
Distinguish an advance statement (wishes) from a legally binding advance decision to refuse treatment.

references.label: NICE NG31 / End of life care guidance

title: Breaking bad news (SPIKES framework)
summary: SPIKES is a six-step protocol for delivering bad news in a structured, compassionate way that supports the patient and plans next steps.

steps.detail: Arrange privacy, adequate time, sit down, minimise interruptions and involve support people the patient wants.
Ask what the patient already knows or suspects before telling ('ask before you tell').
Ask how much information the patient wants to receive.
Give a warning shot, then deliver information in small chunks using plain language; check understanding.
Acknowledge and respond to emotions with empathic statements; allow silence.
Summarise, agree a plan and next steps, and check the patient's understanding and support needs.

references.label: Baile et al. SPIKES - A Six-Step Protocol for Delivering Bad News (The Oncologist, 2000)

title: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) adherence counselling
summary: High, sustained adherence to ART is essential to achieve viral suppression, prevent resistance and reduce transmission (undetectable = untransmittable). Counselling should be supportive, practical and ongoing.

sections.heading: Key messages
items: Take ART every day exactly as prescribed, ideally at the same time.
Good adherence suppresses the virus, protects the immune system and prevents sexual transmission when undetectable (U=U).
Missing doses risks treatment failure and drug resistance.
Attend appointments for viral load monitoring and refills.

steps.detail: Explore stigma, disclosure, side effects, mental health, substance use and practical barriers.
Use reminders, pill boxes, links to daily routines, and treatment supporters.
Reinforce at each visit, manage side effects, and act on raised viral load promptly.

redFlags: Rising or detectable viral load on treatment - assess adherence and consider resistance testing/regimen review.

references.label: WHO Consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment

title: Tuberculosis treatment adherence counselling
summary: TB treatment requires several months of multidrug therapy; completing the full course is essential to cure and prevent drug-resistant TB. Counselling supports completion and early recognition of problems.

sections.heading: Key messages
items: Take all TB medicines every day for the full duration, even when feeling better.
Stopping early can cause relapse and drug-resistant TB.
Attend all reviews and sputum checks; complete the standard 6-month (or as prescribed) course.
Cover coughs and ensure household contacts/children are screened.

steps.detail: Explain the disease, treatment length and importance of completion.
Use treatment supporters/DOT or digital adherence tools per local policy.
Counsel on side effects (e.g. report jaundice, visual changes, severe rash) and review regularly.

redFlags: Report jaundice, severe vomiting, vision changes (ethambutol) or severe rash - may indicate drug toxicity needing review.

references.label: WHO Consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis treatment

title: Antihypertensive adherence counselling
summary: Hypertension is usually symptomless but, untreated, leads to stroke, heart and kidney disease. Long-term adherence to medication and lifestyle change is the key message.

sections.heading: Key messages
items: High blood pressure usually has no symptoms - do not stop medicines because you feel well.
Take medication daily and continue long-term unless advised otherwise.
Reduce salt, maintain a healthy weight, be physically active, limit alcohol and stop smoking.
Attend reviews for blood pressure monitoring.

sections.heading: Support
items: Address side effects and simplify regimens (e.g. once-daily, combination pills) to aid adherence.
Use home BP monitoring where appropriate.
Reinforce that treatment reduces stroke and heart attack risk.

references.label: WHO Guideline for the pharmacological treatment of hypertension in adults

title: Inhaler technique counselling
summary: Poor inhaler technique is a common cause of uncontrolled asthma and COPD. Checking and teaching technique at every opportunity improves drug delivery and control.

steps.detail: Remove cap, shake the inhaler and (if new/unused) prime it; sit or stand upright.
Breathe out gently, away from the inhaler.
Seal lips around the mouthpiece, start a slow deep breath in and press the canister once at the same time. Use a spacer where possible.
Hold breath about 10 seconds, breathe out gently; wait about 30 seconds before a second puff. Rinse mouth after inhaled corticosteroids.

redFlags: Worsening symptoms or high reliever use despite good technique needs medical review and possible treatment step-up.

references.label: NICE/BTS-SIGN Asthma guidance

title: Insulin injection technique and site rotation
summary: Correct subcutaneous injection technique and rotating sites prevent lipohypertrophy and erratic absorption, improving glycaemic control and safety.

steps.detail: Wash hands; for cloudy insulin gently roll/resuspend; attach a new needle and prime to remove air.
Inject into subcutaneous fat (abdomen, thighs, buttocks, upper arms) using a short needle, usually at 90 degrees; a skin fold may be used with longer needles.
Keep the needle in for about 10 seconds after pressing the plunger, then withdraw.

sections.heading: Site rotation and safety
items: Rotate injection sites systematically within a region and between regions to avoid lipohypertrophy.
Use a new needle each time and inspect sites for lumps.
Store insulin correctly (in-use pen at room temperature, spares refrigerated, do not freeze).

redFlags: Injecting into lipohypertrophic lumps causes unpredictable absorption and hypo/hyperglycaemia - avoid and reassess.

references.label: Diabetes UK / FIT injection technique guidance

title: Oral anticoagulation counselling (warfarin and DOACs)
summary: Anticoagulants prevent clots but increase bleeding risk; safe use needs adherence, monitoring (for warfarin) and awareness of interactions and bleeding signs.

sections.heading: Warfarin
items: Take the same time each day; dose is adjusted to the INR - attend monitoring appointments.
Keep vitamin K intake (green leafy vegetables) consistent rather than avoiding it.
Many drugs, alcohol and some supplements interact - check before starting/stopping medicines.
Carry an anticoagulant alert card.

sections.heading: DOACs and general bleeding safety
items: Take DOACs exactly as prescribed (some with food); do not miss doses, but do not double up - follow specific missed-dose advice.
Report any significant or unusual bleeding promptly.
Tell all healthcare and dental staff you take an anticoagulant before procedures.
Do not start new medicines (including over-the-counter NSAIDs) without checking.

redFlags: Seek urgent care for major bleeding, black/tarry stools, blood in urine/vomit, severe headache or a significant head injury.

references.label: NICE Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management (NG196)

title: Smoking cessation counselling (5 A's)
summary: The 5 A's is a brief, evidence-based framework for delivering smoking cessation support in routine consultations.

steps.detail: Ask about tobacco use at every visit and record status.
Give clear, personalised advice to quit and explain the benefits.
Assess willingness/readiness to quit.
For those ready, help make a quit plan; offer behavioural support and pharmacotherapy (e.g. NRT, varenicline/cytisine, bupropion).
Arrange follow-up to support and prevent relapse; refer to cessation services.

references.label: WHO Toolkit for delivering the 5A's and 5R's brief tobacco interventions

title: Safe medication storage counselling
summary: Safe storage prevents accidental poisoning (especially in children), maintains drug effectiveness and reduces misuse. Simple advice protects households.

sections.heading: Key advice
items: Keep all medicines out of sight and reach of children, ideally in a locked or high cupboard.
Store in original labelled containers; keep child-resistant caps closed.
Follow storage conditions (cool, dry, away from sunlight; refrigerate where required - do not freeze unless instructed).
Check expiry dates and return unused/expired medicines to a pharmacy for safe disposal.
Never share prescription medicines with others.

redFlags: Suspected accidental ingestion (especially in a child) - seek urgent medical/poisons advice immediately.

references.label: WHO/CDC safe medicine storage guidance

title: Oral rehydration solution (ORS) preparation at home
summary: ORS prevents and treats dehydration from diarrhoea cheaply and effectively. Correct preparation and giving are essential - too concentrated a solution is dangerous.

steps.detail: Dissolve one ORS sachet in the exact volume of clean (boiled and cooled or safe) water stated on the packet (commonly 1 litre). Do not add extra sugar or salt.
If no sachet, mix six level teaspoons of sugar and half a level teaspoon of salt in one litre of clean water (use accurate measures).
Give frequent small sips/spoonfuls after each loose stool; continue breastfeeding and feeding. Make a fresh solution every 24 hours.

redFlags: Seek care for danger signs: persistent vomiting, blood in stool, sunken eyes, no urine, lethargy, or inability to drink - the child may need IV fluids or zinc and assessment.

references.label: WHO Oral rehydration salts: production of the new ORS

title: Danger signs in pregnancy and newborn (when to return)
summary: Teaching mothers and families to recognise danger signs and seek care promptly saves lives. Counselling should cover both maternal and newborn warning signs.

sections.heading: Maternal danger signs - go to a facility urgently
items: Vaginal bleeding.
Convulsions/fits.
Severe headache with blurred vision.
Fever and too weak to get out of bed.
Severe abdominal pain.
Fast or difficult breathing; swelling of face/hands with these symptoms.

sections.heading: Newborn danger signs - seek care immediately
items: Not feeding well / unable to breastfeed.
Convulsions.
Fast breathing (60 breaths/min or more) or severe chest in-drawing.
Fever (>=37.5 C) or low temperature (<35.5 C).
No or reduced movement / very lethargic.
Jaundice (yellow) in the first 24 hours, or yellow palms and soles; umbilical redness/pus.

redFlags: Any maternal or newborn danger sign warrants immediate transfer to a health facility.

references.label: WHO Pregnancy, childbirth, postpartum and newborn care guide

title: Diabetic foot care counselling
summary: Daily foot care and early detection of problems prevent diabetic foot ulcers and amputations in people with diabetes, particularly those with neuropathy or poor circulation.

sections.heading: Daily care
items: Inspect both feet every day (use a mirror or ask for help) for cuts, blisters, redness, swelling or colour change.
Wash feet daily with lukewarm water (check temperature with the hand/elbow), dry well including between toes, and moisturise dry skin (not between toes).
Cut/file nails straight across; do not cut corners.
Always wear well-fitting footwear and never walk barefoot; check inside shoes before wearing.

sections.heading: When to seek help
items: Report any new ulcer, wound, blister, redness, swelling, or change in colour/temperature promptly.
Do not use corn/callus removers or attempt to cut corns yourself.
Attend regular foot checks per your diabetes care plan.

redFlags: New ulcer, spreading redness, warmth, swelling, pus, foul smell, or black tissue - seek urgent care (possible infection or critical ischaemia).

references.label: NICE Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management (NG19)

title: Contraception counselling (method choice)
summary: Effective contraception counselling is person-centred and supports informed choice across all suitable methods, including the most effective long-acting reversible methods, guided by the WHO MEC.

sections.heading: What to cover
items: Explore the person's needs, preferences, plans for future pregnancy and any medical conditions.
Discuss the full range of methods, presenting the most effective (LARC) options proactively.
Explain effectiveness (typical vs perfect use), how to use, common side effects and what to do if a dose/method fails.
Apply WHO MEC to identify safe methods for the individual's conditions.
Emphasise dual protection: condoms for STI prevention alongside another method.

redFlags: Screen for conditions that make some methods unsafe (e.g. migraine with aura, VTE history) before recommending combined hormonal methods.

references.label: WHO Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 5th ed (2015)

title: Immunisation counselling and vaccine hesitancy
summary: Addressing vaccine hesitancy with empathetic, accurate, tailored communication improves vaccine confidence and uptake. A presumptive, respectful approach that addresses specific concerns works best.

sections.heading: Approach
items: Use a presumptive recommendation ('your child is due for these vaccines today') while remaining respectful of questions.
Listen to and acknowledge specific concerns without dismissing them.
Give clear, accurate information on benefits, common mild side effects and the risks of the disease.
Use trusted sources and tailor to the individual's concerns and culture; offer follow-up.
Make vaccination easy (timing, access) and document discussions.

sections.heading: Key messages
items: Vaccines are rigorously tested and continuously monitored for safety.
Most side effects are mild and short-lived; serious reactions are rare.
Vaccination protects the individual and the wider community.

references.label: WHO Vaccine hesitancy and demand resources
